samples.task_summary: Predict whether a worker’s one-way commute to work exceeds the ACS travel-time threshold, using person and work-related attributes that should generalize across states.

scores.rationale: Age plausibly affects job type, mode choice, and residential-work patterns, but its relationship to long commute is moderate rather than dominant and should generalize reasonably well.
Education is a fairly stable proxy for occupation, earnings, and urban labor-market sorting, all of which can influence commute length across states.
Marital status may correlate with household location choices and work arrangements, but effects are indirect and weaker for commute-time prediction.
Sex can correlate with occupation mix and commuting patterns, but it is a sensitive demographic shortcut with limited stable marginal usefulness.
Disability status can affect labor-force attachment, feasible commute modes, and job selection, giving some stable signal without being central.
Parental employment status is mainly relevant for children and should have little meaningful or stable predictive value for workers’ commute time.
Recent mobility may indicate residential change and job-location mismatch, which can affect commute time, though coding may also reflect heterogeneous life events.
Relationship to householder captures household role and life stage, which can influence where people live relative to work, but only indirectly.
Race may correlate with segregation and labor-market structure, but it is a sensitive shortcut and likely to encode state-specific social patterns rather than robust causal signal.
Residence PUMA is a fine-grained geographic identifier that strongly encodes local domain and is unlikely to generalize out of state.
State directly identifies the domain and would be a brittle shortcut for an out-of-distribution across-state generalization setting.
Citizenship status may weakly proxy for labor-market segment and residential sorting, but much of its signal is indirect and potentially confounded with geography.
Occupation is one of the most stable predictors because commute length depends strongly on job type, work location patterns, and industry-specific commuting norms across states.
Commute mode is extremely informative for travel time and should remain semantically predictive across states despite some geographic variation in mode prevalence.
Place-of-work PUMA is another fine-grained geographic code that effectively leaks local spatial structure and is highly brittle across states.
Income-to-poverty ratio is a stable socioeconomic indicator tied to housing-job tradeoffs, vehicle access, and urban sorting, making it broadly useful across states.

samples.task_summary: Predict whether a worker’s commute travel time falls above the acstraveltime threshold using person, job, and commute-related ACS features.

scores.rationale: Age has some broad association with job type, residential choice, and commuting patterns, but its marginal effect on commute duration is modest and indirect across states.
Education is moderately informative through occupation and urban labor-market sorting, but much of its signal is mediated by other variables and can vary by state context.
Marital status may weakly track household location and work arrangements, yet it is only indirectly related to commute time and not especially robust marginally.
Sex can correlate with labor-force patterns and commute behavior, but it is a sensitive demographic shortcut with limited stable causal relevance to travel time itself.
Disability status may affect employment type, commute feasibility, and mode choice, giving some real signal, though it remains indirect and potentially entangled with selection into work.
Parental employment status is mainly defined for children and should have little meaningful stable value for a worker commute-time task.
Recent mobility may weakly indicate residential instability or long-distance adjustment, but it is not a core determinant of current commute duration and may be noisy.
Relationship to householder can reflect household structure and residential constraints, yet it is only a weak proxy for commute time and likely less stable than job-related features.
Race often acts as a demographic shortcut tied to segregation and local structure rather than a stable semantic driver, so it should be heavily downweighted for OOD generalization.
Home PUMA is a fine-grained geographic identifier that strongly encodes local domain and state-specific commuting infrastructure, making it highly brittle out of distribution.
State directly identifies the domain and would act as a geography shortcut rather than a transferable predictor.
Citizenship status may correlate with job sorting and residence patterns, but it is mostly an indirect demographic proxy and not a stable semantic cause of commute duration.
Occupation is one of the most plausibly stable predictors because different jobs systematically imply different work locations, schedules, and commuting patterns across states.
Transportation mode is directly tied to commute duration and should remain highly predictive across states, making it the strongest stable feature despite some local variation.
Workplace PUMA is another detailed geographic code that can nearly localize commute structure, so it is powerful in-domain but highly non-transferable and shortcut-prone.
Income-to-poverty ratio provides moderate stable signal through residential location, car access, and job type, though much of its effect is indirect and geography-mediated.

  once and do not include feature names in the output.
